newsitem.title: USA: AT&T, Bell Atlantic, NYNEX have access reform plan.
newsitem.headline: AT&T, Bell Atlantic, NYNEX have access reform plan.

text.p: AT&T Corp., Bell Atlantic Corp, and NYNEX Corp proposed a plan Friday that would cut the charges long-distance carriers pay to access the local phone network by $2.5 billion a year and cut consumer phone bills by more than $400 million a year.

In an unusual accord, the three companies sketched out a compromise for how the Federal Communications Commission could reduce access charges and overhaul the system that ensures Americans get quality and affordable phone service.

The FCC is struggling to develop proposals by early next month that attempt to take into consideration the demands of the local and long-distance phone industries -- which have been waging a bitter ad campaign over the issues.
The joint proposal could help break the logjam.
Officials at the companies, in a joint teleconference with reporters, said their proposal would:
-- Cut by 45 percent, to 1.5 cents a minute from 2.7 cents, the fees long-distance companies pay the regional Baby Bell phone companies and other local carriers for access to the local network.
-- Expand funding to ensure that basic phone service is available to high-cost rural communities and low-income communities.
-- Fund a $2.3 billion plan proposed last year by federal and state regulators to link schools and libraries to the Internet at discounted rates.
Local carriers at the same time would boost the ceiling on subscriber line charges for business customers to $6 from $3.50 for a single line, and to $8 from $6 for multiple lines.
AT&T, meanwhile, reaffirmed a commitment to pass along to consumers and business -- dollar for dollar in the form of lower long-distance phone rates -- any cut in access charges.

To cover the cost of hooking up schools, libraries and others to the Internet, the carriers proposed a monthly fee of 75 cents a line for all customers. This "Connect America" fee would be phased in via three 25-cent installments between July 1997 and July 1998.

To contribute to the reduction in access charges, the carriers proposed a "presubscribed line charge" that would be billed to long-distance carriers. It would amount to $1 a month for residential lines and $2 a month for business lines and take effect on January 1, 1998.
There would be no increase in the $3.50 monthly subscriber line charge now paid by phone customers.
Consumer advocates reacted negatively to the plan.

"It is absolutely crazy to raise consumers' local charges $3 billion a year at a time when costs are declining and competition should be driving out inefficiencies in telephone pricing," said Gene Kimmelman, co-director of the Washington office of Consumers Union.
The $3 billion refers to the 75-cent Connect America fee and the $1 presubscribed line charge. Kimmelman said the latter would be passed to consumers by long-distance carriers.
Other local carriers gave a guarded response.
Roy Neel, president of the United States Telephone Association, called the proposal "a significant departure" from his trade group's stated positions on access charge and universal service reform.
He said his group's members -- which are local carriers -- are analyzing the plan to "understand the implications of its various components."
